advances: Arbitrary barycentric relations between positive-volume fibers admit joint laws with every prescribed uniform marginal and a common uniform target-fiber reference, with a density cost determined by the arithmetic mean of the volume roots. This gives a common target-centroid metronoid core and a globally capacity-feasible depth certificate charging average cost. The certificate admits an exact finite cutoff packing formulation and dual after reducing source supports to affinely independent sets of size at most \(n+1\). No universal lower bound for the resulting scalar packing score is asserted.
author: research-agent
external_sources:
Robert J. McCann, [A Convexity Principle for Interacting Gases](https://www.math.toronto.edu/~mccann/papers/advances.pdf), Advances in Mathematics 128 (1997), 153-179, [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1006/aima.1997.1634). Definition 1.1 and equation (7) provide a convex-potential gradient transport \(T\) between absolutely continuous probability laws. Proposition 1.3(ii) gives absolute continuity of its displacement interpolants. The \(q=\infty\) case of Theorem 2.3, printed page 164, is exactly (11). This is the external input already recorded in accepted fact `dfd25e72c1f45a4e`. Every endpoint used here is an absolutely continuous probability law with bounded measurable density and compact support; the inductive bound (12) checks this for intermediate endpoints. No smoothness or strict positivity of the densities is required. The transport map is needed only almost everywhere under its source law.

The uniform centroid inequality and compact convexity of metronoids are used through accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d`. The measurable bounded-domination depth bound is used through the independent probability statement of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`. The entropy argument of accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194` is extended in (15)-(16) with the regularity and positivity arguments given above. There are no other external inputs.
proof:
Compactness of the base projection of \(C\) implies that only finitely many lattice fibers are nonempty. Every positive-volume fiber is a compact full-dimensional convex set. Thus the stated uniform laws exist, and all measures considered below have compact support. We work with \(W>0\) until the final zero-volume observation.

For the coupling construction, use the displacement-interpolation input stated and applied in the proof of accepted fact `dfd25e72c1f45a4e`. For two absolutely continuous probability densities \(f_0,f_1\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\), its transport map \(T\) sends the first law to the second, and the density \(f_t\) of \((1-t)\mathbf X+tT(\mathbf X)\) satisfies

\[
\|f_t\|_\infty^{-1/d}
\ge(1-t)\|f_0\|_\infty^{-1/d}
+t\|f_1\|_\infty^{-1/d}
\quad(0\le t\le1).
\tag{11}
\]

The exact primary source and its applicability to merely measurable densities are specified below.

First merge repeated source indices, if any. Adding their coefficients preserves both the base barycenter and \(V_\lambda\). A coupling for the distinct indices gives one for the original list by assigning the same random vector to all copies of each index. Every listed coordinate then has its prescribed uniform marginal, and the weighted output is unchanged. We may therefore construct the coupling for a list of distinct sources.

Put \(b_i=\sum_{j=1}^i\lambda_j\). Start with \(\mathbf X_1\sim U_{\mathbf I_1}\), and set \(\mathbf B_1=\mathbf X_1\). Suppose a joint law of \((\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_{i-1})\) has been constructed, with the required marginals, and its normalized weighted average \(\mathbf B_{i-1}=b_{i-1}^{-1}\sum_{j<i}\lambda_j\mathbf X_j\) has a bounded density \(f_{i-1}\). Apply (11) to its law and \(U_{\mathbf I_i}\), choosing a transport map \(T_i\). Extend the existing joint law by the measurable assignment \(\mathbf X_i=T_i(\mathbf B_{i-1})\). A map defined almost everywhere for the law of \(\mathbf B_{i-1}\) may be defined arbitrarily on its null exceptional set. The projection of this enlarged law to all its old coordinates is exactly the old joint law, while its new marginal is \(U_{\mathbf I_i}\).

For \(i\ge2\), both \(b_{i-1}/b_i\) and \(\lambda_i/b_i\) lie strictly between zero and one and sum to one. The next average is precisely the displacement interpolant

\[
\mathbf B_i
=\frac{b_{i-1}}{b_i}\mathbf B_{i-1}
+\frac{\lambda_i}{b_i}T_i(\mathbf B_{i-1}).
\]

Its density \(f_i\) therefore exists and, by induction from \(\|f_1\|_\infty=w_{\mathbf I_1}^{-1}\), obeys

\[
\|f_i\|_\infty^{-1/d}
\ge\frac{b_{i-1}}{b_i}\|f_{i-1}\|_\infty^{-1/d}
+\frac{\lambda_i}{b_i}w_{\mathbf I_i}^{1/d}
\ge\frac1{b_i}\sum_{j\le i}\lambda_jw_{\mathbf I_j}^{1/d}.
\tag{12}
\]

All intermediate averages have compact support because they are weighted averages of samples from the fixed compact fibers. The induction thus verifies every hypothesis of each transport invocation. Since \(b_s=1\), (12) gives the bound \(V_\lambda^{-1}\) on the final density. Convexity of \(C\) gives \(\sum_i\lambda_i C_{\mathbf I_i}\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\), so the output is carried by that fiber. Integrating its density yields \(1\le w_{\mathbf J}/V_\lambda\), proving both (1) and target positivity. The case \(s=1\) is the original uniform law with \(\mathbf J=\mathbf I_1\), \(V_\lambda=w_{\mathbf J}\), and \(L_\lambda=0\). Deleting zero coefficients leaves a nonempty list since the coefficient sum is one; independent extra coordinates do not alter that output or any old marginal.

Weighted arithmetic-geometric mean applied to the positive numbers \(w_{\mathbf I_i}^{1/d}\) gives \(d\log(\sum_i\lambda_iw_{\mathbf I_i}^{1/d})\ge\sum_i\lambda_i\log w_{\mathbf I_i}\). This and \(w_{\mathbf J}\ge V_\lambda\) prove (2).

We next prove the common-core assertion. Target positivity follows by applying (1) to any representation in the nonempty set \(\Lambda_{\mathbf J}(E)\). Fix one such representation and use only its positive support. By (2) and the root-volume hypothesis, choose its coupling with \(P_\lambda\le R U_{\mathbf J}\). The centroid \(\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}\) belongs to \(\mathsf M_{w_{\mathbf J}}(C_{\mathbf J})\), using the density one in (3). Accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d` therefore gives \(U_{\mathbf J}(G)\ge\gamma_d\) for every closed halfspace \(G\) containing this centroid.

Fix \(\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) and take \(G=\{\mathbf y:\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf y\rangle\ge\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}\rangle\}\). Domination on its complement gives

\[
P_\lambda(G)
=1-P_\lambda(G^c)
\ge1-RU_{\mathbf J}(G^c)
\ge1-R(1-\gamma_d)=\theta.
\tag{13}
\]

Let \(A\) be the event in the product probability space that the weighted output belongs to \(G\). The measure \(\eta=(\theta/\Pi_\lambda(A))\mathbf1_A\Pi_\lambda\) is a submeasure of \(\Pi_\lambda\), has mass exactly \(\theta\), and is carried by that event. Each source marginal \(\eta_{\mathbf I}\) has mass \(\theta\) and is dominated by \(U_{\mathbf I}\). Hence \(w_{\mathbf I}\eta_{\mathbf I}\le\mu_{\mathbf I}\) has mass \(\theta w_{\mathbf I}\), and its normalized barycenter
\(\mathbf q_{\mathbf I}=\theta^{-1}\int\mathbf y\,d\eta_{\mathbf I}(\mathbf y)\) belongs to \(\mathsf M_{\theta w_{\mathbf I}}(C_{\mathbf I})\). These metronoids are valid because \(0<\theta\le\gamma_d<1\). Integration over \(A\) gives

\[
\left\langle\mathbf v,
\sum_{\mathbf I}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\mathbf q_{\mathbf I}\right\rangle
\ge\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}\rangle.
\tag{14}
\]

By accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d`, each metronoid is nonempty, compact, and convex, so its indicated finite Minkowski sum has these properties. Formula (14) shows that its support function is at least \(\langle\mathbf v,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}\rangle\) in every nonzero direction, and the zero direction is automatic. Strict separation of a point from a compact convex set proves membership of the centroid in that sum. The representation was arbitrary, so (4) follows. The points used to establish support-function inequalities may depend on the direction; separation is what gives actual membership. The centroid is fixed across all representations, and the auxiliary measures for separate representations are not summed as a capacity scheme.

We establish (7), including the regularity that cannot be obtained by simply deleting the continuity hypothesis of accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194`. In this argument \(Q\) is the uniform law on \(K\), and write \(\mathcal D=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) for the entropy scalar denoted \(D\) in that predecessor. Since \(P\) has a bounded measurable density supported in \(K\), its density ratio with respect to \(Q\) is bounded. Thus \(\mathcal D\) is finite: the function \(t\log t\), with \(0\log0=0\), is bounded above and below on the relevant bounded interval.

For \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\mathbf u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}\), let \(G(\mathbf x,\mathbf u)=\{\mathbf y:\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf y-\mathbf x\rangle\ge0\}\). Every closed halfspace containing \(\mathbf x\) contains such a through-point halfspace. Along any convergent sequence of pairs \((\mathbf x,\mathbf u)\), their indicators converge outside the limiting boundary hyperplane. That hyperplane is \(P\)-null by absolute continuity. Dominated convergence proves joint continuity of \(P(G(\mathbf x,\mathbf u))\). Compactness of the sphere gives
\(\operatorname{TD}_P(\mathbf x)=\min_{\mathbf u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}P(G(\mathbf x,\mathbf u))\). Uniform continuity on a compact neighborhood of any point times the sphere proves continuity of this minimum in \(\mathbf x\).

The convex hull \(K_P=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}P)\) is compact and lies in \(K\). Strict separation supplies a through-point halfspace of probability zero at every point outside \(K_P\). The global maximum depth is consequently attained on \(K_P\). It is positive without any continuity assumption on the density: at the mean \(\mathbf m=\int\mathbf y\,dP(\mathbf y)\), each through-point halfspace has positive probability. Otherwise the bounded random variable \(\langle\mathbf u,\mathbf Y-\mathbf m\rangle\) would be strictly negative almost surely and have negative expectation, contradicting its zero expectation. Joint continuity and compactness of the sphere make the minimum of these positive probabilities positive. Opposite through-point halfspaces have probabilities summing to one, since their common hyperplane is null. Thus the attained maximum \(\delta\) satisfies \(0<\delta\le1/2\).

Set \(r=\lfloor1/(2\delta)\rfloor\). Then \(1/(4\delta)\le r\le1/(2\delta)\) and \(r\ge1\). We give the entropy cutting argument directly with compact convex remainders. Start with \(K_0=K\). Suppose \(i<r\) and \(P(K_i)\ge1-i\delta\). This lower bound is positive, so \(K_i\) has positive volume by absolute continuity of \(P\). It is a convex body. Let \(\mathbf c_i\) be its uniform centroid. Choose a minimizing direction at \(\mathbf c_i\) and write \(G_i=G(\mathbf c_i,\mathbf u_i)\), so \(P(G_i)=\operatorname{TD}_P(\mathbf c_i)\le\delta\). The point \(\mathbf c_i\) need not belong to \(K_P\); the inequality uses the global maximum \(\delta\).

Accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d`, applied at full metronoid mass \(\mathcal L^d(K_i)\), gives \(\mathcal L^d(K_i\cap G_i)\ge\gamma_d\mathcal L^d(K_i)\). Also \(\gamma_d\ge e^{-1}\), since \(d\log(1+1/d)\le1\). Put \(K_{i+1}=K_i\cap\{\mathbf y:\langle\mathbf u_i,\mathbf y-\mathbf c_i\rangle\le0\}\). The common cutting hyperplane has zero Lebesgue and \(P\) measure, so

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(K_{i+1})&\ge P(K_i)-P(G_i)\ge1-(i+1)\delta,\\
Q(K_{i+1})&\le(1-e^{-1})Q(K_i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]

The first bound stays at least \(1/2\) through step \(r\), justifying positive volume and every centroid used in the induction. At the end, \(p=P(K_r)\ge1/2\) and \(0<q=Q(K_r)\le e^{-\ell r}<1\). Jensen's inequality for \(t\log t\), applied separately under \(Q\) conditioned on \(K_r\) and its complement, yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D
&\ge p\log\frac pq+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q},\\
\mathcal D+\log2
&\ge p\log\frac1q
\ge\frac{\ell r}{2}
\ge\frac{\ell}{8\delta}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]

The convention \(0\log0=0\) includes \(p=1\); the second line uses \(p\log p+(1-p)\log(1-p)\ge-\log2\) and \((1-p)\log(1/(1-q))\ge0\). Jensen under \(Q\) also gives \(\mathcal D\ge0\), so rearrangement is valid. Choosing the already established maximizer of depth proves (7). This proves the needed extension of the predecessor's entropy argument with all density regularity and attainment steps included.

Now fix a scheme (5), discard its zero-mass components, and choose for each remaining component a coupling from (1). Denote its output by \(P_a\), and set \(\pi_a=x_a\Pi_a\) and \(\sigma=x_\circ U_{\mathbf J}\). At any \(\mathbf I\in D\), the aggregate source usage is exactly

\[
\mathbf1_{\{\mathbf I=\mathbf J\}}\sigma
+\sum_{a:\mathbf I\in E_a}(\pi_a)_{\mathbf I}
=\left(\mathbf1_{\{\mathbf I=\mathbf J\}}x_\circ
+\sum_{a:\mathbf I\in E_a}x_a\right)U_{\mathbf I}
\le\mu_{\mathbf I}.
\tag{17}
\]

Here the central term is zero unless \(\mathbf I=\mathbf J\), and \((\pi_a)_{\mathbf I}\) denotes the corresponding marginal. This verifies all measure capacities simultaneously, not merely total masses in separate components. Summing (5) over \(D\) gives \(x_\circ+\sum_a|E_a|x_a\le W\), hence \(M\le W\).

The barycentric output measure and its normalized law are

\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}=x_\circ U_{\mathbf J}+\sum_a x_aP_a,
\qquad
P=\frac{\kappa_{\mathbf J}}M.
\tag{18}
\]

By (2), each \(P_a\le e^{L_a}U_{\mathbf J}\). All costs are finite and nonnegative, so this finite mixture has a bounded measurable density supported in \(C_{\mathbf J}\). Moreover, \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_a\|U_{\mathbf J})\le L_a\), since \(\log(dP_a/dU_{\mathbf J})\le L_a\) \(P_a\)-almost everywhere. Pointwise convexity of \(t\log t\) applied to the density ratios in (18), followed by integration, proves

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|U_{\mathbf J})
\le\frac{x_\circ}{M}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(U_{\mathbf J}\|U_{\mathbf J})
+\sum_a\frac{x_a}{M}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_a\|U_{\mathbf J})
\le\frac{S_{\mathrm{cost}}}{M}.
\tag{19}
\]

Applying (7) with \(K=C_{\mathbf J}\) and \(Q=U_{\mathbf J}\) supplies one \(\mathbf y^\star\in C_{\mathbf J}\) whose \(P\)-depth is at least \(\ell/[8(S_{\mathrm{cost}}/M+\log2)]\).

To transfer this depth, consider any closed ambient halfspace \(H=\{(\mathbf z,\mathbf y):\langle\mathbf a,\mathbf z\rangle+\langle\mathbf b,\mathbf y\rangle\ge t\}\), with \((\mathbf a,\mathbf b)\ne(\mathbf0,\mathbf0)\), and put \(H_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in H\}\). In a component, the score at the barycentric output equals the weighted sum of the source scores. If every source score is strictly negative, that weighted sum is strictly negative. Therefore, including equality cases,

\[
\mathbf1_{H_{\mathbf J}}
\left(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E_a}\lambda_{a,\mathbf I}\mathbf y_{\mathbf I}\right)
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in E_a}\mathbf1_{H_{\mathbf I}}(\mathbf y_{\mathbf I}).
\tag{20}
\]

Integrating against \(\pi_a\), adding the central contribution, and using (17) gives, for every such \(H\),

\[
\kappa_{\mathbf J}(H_{\mathbf J})
\le\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}\mu_{\mathbf I}(H_{\mathbf I})
=\mathcal H_d(S\cap H).
\tag{21}
\]

If \(H\) contains \((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star)\) and \(\mathbf b\ne\mathbf0\), its section \(H_{\mathbf J}\) is a proper closed halfspace containing \(\mathbf y^\star\). If \(\mathbf b=\mathbf0\), that section is all of \(\mathbb R^d\), so its output mass is \(M\). Thus the depth guarantee at the same fixed point and (21) prove (6) for every containing ambient halfspace, including vertical ones. There is no assumption that ambient boundary hyperplanes have zero mixed volume. If the whole space is admitted as an improper halfspace, its mass \(W\ge M\) suffices as well.

For the cutoff bound, if every positive-mass \(L_a\le L\), (18) gives \(P\le e^L U_{\mathbf J}\). The independent probability statement of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`, with its \(\nu=P\) and \(Q=U_{\mathbf J}\), supplies a depth maximizer in \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}P)\subseteq C_{\mathbf J}\) of depth at least \(1/[6(1+L)]\). Its hypotheses hold because the uniform reference is compactly supported with a measurable log-concave density, and domination is a Borel measure inequality. Apply (21) at that point exactly as above to obtain \(M/[6(1+L)]\).

If \(S_{\mathrm{cost}}=0\), nonnegativity of the costs implies \(L_a=0\) whenever \(x_a>0\). A probability measure \(P_a\le U_{\mathbf J}\) must equal \(U_{\mathbf J}\), since the nonnegative difference has total mass zero. Hence \(\kappa_{\mathbf J}=M U_{\mathbf J}\). The centroid bound from accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d`, followed by (21), gives \(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}))\ge\gamma_d M\).

For the arity reduction, fix a component support \(E\) and maximize the linear functional \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\alpha_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}\) over its barycentric polytope \(\Lambda_{\mathbf J}(E)\). This polytope is nonempty, compact, and convex, so an optimizer exists. Among optimizers choose one with the fewest positive coordinates, and call its positive support \(E'\). If \(E'\) were affinely dependent, there would be a nonzero vector \((v_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in E'}\) with \(\sum v_{\mathbf I}=0\) and \(\sum v_{\mathbf I}\mathbf I=\mathbf0\). Both sufficiently small perturbations \(\alpha\pm\varepsilon v\) are feasible. Optimality forces \(\sum v_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}=0\), since otherwise one of these perturbations increases the objective. Move along one such direction until the first positive coordinate becomes zero. This is possible because a nonzero vector with coordinate sum zero has a positive and a negative coordinate. Feasibility and optimality are preserved, contradicting minimal positive support.

Thus \(E'\subseteq E\) is affinely independent, \(|E'|\le n+1\), and its coefficients are the unique barycentric coordinates of \(\mathbf J\) in that simplex. They are positive, so \(\mathbf J\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}E'\). The root-volume mean has weakly increased, so its cost has weakly decreased. Retaining component mass \(x\) and replacing \(E\) by \(E'\) changes source usage from \(x\mathbf1_E\) to \(x\mathbf1_{E'}\), a coordinatewise decrease. If \(E'=\{\mathbf J\}\), the same mass can instead be added to \(x_\circ\), with exactly the same remaining source usage. Applying this operation independently to every component preserves global feasibility and total mass, and weakly decreases the total cost.

There are only finitely many subsets of \(D\), so \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) is finite. All its costs are finite and nonnegative by (1). At a fixed cutoff, replacing each component as above and grouping identical reduced supports yields a feasible vector in (8) of exactly the original mass. All reduced costs remain below the same cutoff. Conversely, a feasible vector in (8) gives a scheme (5), taking the singleton variable as central mass and using the unique coefficients on every other set. This proves the asserted exact correspondence of optimal masses, including arbitrary original source arities and repeated supports.

The feasible region of (8) is nonempty and compact: the zero vector is feasible, and each coordinate is bounded by \(\min_{\mathbf I\in E}w_{\mathbf I}\), because every support is nonempty. Thus the maximum is attained. Taking mass \(w_{\mathbf J}\) on the central singleton shows \(P_d(\mathbf J,L)\ge w_{\mathbf J}>0\), and summing capacities gives \(P_d(\mathbf J,L)\le W\).

For completeness, the dual equality and its attainment follow directly from separation. Let \(A\) be the finite incidence matrix whose columns are the vectors \(\mathbf1_E\) for the allowed supports, and let \(p\) be the primal maximum. Weak duality follows from \(A x\le w\), \(A^{\mathsf T}u\ge\mathbf1\), and nonnegativity. Consider the convex cone generated by \((\mathbf1_E,1)\) for the allowed supports, \((\mathbf e_{\mathbf I},0)\) for \(\mathbf I\in D\), and \((\mathbf0,-1)\). It is closed: a conic representation can be reduced to linearly independent positive generators by eliminating dependencies; consequently the cone is a finite union of the closed cones on linearly independent subsets of these generators. Membership of \((w,t)\) in this cone is equivalent to existence of a feasible \(x\) with \(\sum_E x_E\ge t\).

For \(\varepsilon>0\), the point \((w,p+\varepsilon)\) lies outside the cone. Separation from a closed convex cone gives a linear functional \((b,t)\mapsto u\cdot b-vt\) nonnegative on the cone and strictly negative at this point. Its values on the generators imply \(u\ge0\), \(v\ge0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}u\ge v\mathbf1\). Necessarily \(v>0\), because \(v=0\) would give \(u\cdot w\ge0\), contrary to strict negativity. Normalize to \(v=1\). We have a feasible dual vector with \(u\cdot w<p+\varepsilon\). For a sequence \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) with \(\varepsilon\le1\), all its coordinates are bounded by \((p+1)/w_{\mathbf I}\), since every \(w_{\mathbf I}>0\). A convergent subsequence yields a feasible dual vector with objective at most \(p\), and weak duality forces equality. This proves (9) and attainment without an unverified numerical optimality claim.

For any cutoff \(L\ge0\), the largest attained support cost \(t\le L\) exists because the singleton has cost zero. The allowed supports at \(L\) and \(t\) coincide, so \(P_d(\mathbf J,L)=P_d(\mathbf J,t)\) and \(P_d(\mathbf J,L)/(1+L)\le P_d(\mathbf J,t)/(1+t)\). This reduces the outer maximization to a finite set at each of finitely many targets. Choose a maximizing target and cutoff, then an optimizer of (8), and finally the point supplied by the cutoff depth bound. These choices precede the arbitrary containing halfspace and prove (10). Attainment of \(h_{\max}(C)\) itself is part of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`; (10) already provides the required witness without needing that additional maximization.

If \(W=0\), all mixed halfspace masses are nonnegative and the right side of (10), under its stated convention, is zero. Any point of the assumed nonempty \(S\) works. Zero-volume fibers never enter a normalization or a positive-source capacity scheme. No step above establishes a dimension-independent lower bound of order \(2^{-n}W\) for \(\mathcal B_d(w)\); such a bound would be an additional sufficient bridge to the locked conjecture.
statement:
Let \(n,d\ge1\), let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and retain the locked definitions \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d\), \(S=C\cap\Lambda\), and \(h_S\). Assume \(S\ne\varnothing\). For every lattice index \(\mathbf I\), put \(C_{\mathbf I}=\{\mathbf y:(\mathbf I,\mathbf y)\in C\}\), \(\mu_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal L^d|_{C_{\mathbf I}}\), and \(w_{\mathbf I}=\mu_{\mathbf I}(\mathbb R^d)\). Write \(D=\{\mathbf I\in\mathbb Z^n:w_{\mathbf I}>0\}\) and \(W=\sum_{\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}=\mathcal H_d(S)\). The set \(D\) is finite. When \(W>0\), define \(U_{\mathbf I}=\mu_{\mathbf I}/w_{\mathbf I}\) for \(\mathbf I\in D\). These are the uniform fiber laws denoted \(\lambda_{\mathbf I}\) in the application part of accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`; the symbols \(\lambda_i\) below denote scalar barycentric coefficients. All logarithms are natural. Put \(\gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d\) and \(\ell=-\log(1-e^{-1})\).

First, take any integer \(s\ge1\), indices \(\mathbf I_1,\ldots,\mathbf I_s\in D\), and coefficients \(\lambda_i>0\) with \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), such that \(\mathbf J=\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf I_i\) is an integer vector. There exists a joint probability law \(\Pi_\lambda\) of \((\mathbf X_1,\ldots,\mathbf X_s)\) whose \(i\)-th marginal is exactly \(U_{\mathbf I_i}\), and the law \(P_\lambda\) of \(\sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf X_i\) has a measurable density satisfying

\[
\frac{dP_\lambda}{d\mathcal L^d}
\le \frac{\mathbf1_{C_{\mathbf J}}}{V_\lambda}
\quad\text{a.e.},
\qquad
V_\lambda:=\left(\sum_i\lambda_iw_{\mathbf I_i}^{1/d}\right)^d.
\tag{1}
\]

In particular, \(w_{\mathbf J}\ge V_\lambda>0\), so \(\mathbf J\in D\). With \(L_\lambda=\log(w_{\mathbf J}/V_\lambda)\), one has

\[
0\le L_\lambda
\le \log w_{\mathbf J}-\sum_i\lambda_i\log w_{\mathbf I_i},
\qquad
P_\lambda\le e^{L_\lambda}U_{\mathbf J}
\quad\text{as Borel measures}.
\tag{2}
\]

The recursive construction preserves the entire previously constructed joint law at each stage. Repeated indices are allowed: they may first be merged by adding their coefficients, then recovered by copying the common source variable. Zero coefficients may be deleted; if their indices lie in \(D\), their prescribed uniform variables can also be appended independently. No uniform law is assigned to a zero-volume fiber.

Second, use exactly the metronoid of accepted fact `6769574fc1bd9f8d`: for a convex body \(K\) of positive volume and \(0<m\le\mathcal L^d(K)\),

\[
\mathsf M_m(K)=\left\{
\frac1m\int_K\mathbf y f(\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y:
0\le f\le1\text{ a.e.},\ \int_K f=m
\right\}.
\tag{3}
\]

Let \(E\subseteq D\), let \(\mathbf J\in\mathbb Z^n\cap\operatorname{conv}E\), and let \(\Lambda_{\mathbf J}(E)\) be the set of coefficient vectors \((\lambda_{\mathbf I})_{\mathbf I\in E}\) with nonnegative entries, sum one, and \(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}\lambda_{\mathbf I}\mathbf I=\mathbf J\). In the definitions of \(V_\lambda\) and \(L_\lambda\), omit zero coefficients. Suppose \(R\ge1\), \(\theta=1-R(1-\gamma_d)>0\), and \(V_\lambda\ge w_{\mathbf J}/R\) for every \(\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathbf J}(E)\). Then the actual target-fiber centroid \(\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}=\int\mathbf y\,dU_{\mathbf J}(\mathbf y)\) satisfies

\[
\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}\in
\bigcap_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathbf J}(E)}
\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}
\lambda_{\mathbf I}\mathsf M_{\theta w_{\mathbf I}}(C_{\mathbf I}),
\tag{4}
\]

where a zero scalar multiple of a set means \(\{\mathbf0\}\). Thus the same centroid belongs to every displayed Minkowski sum. The assertion requires \(\theta>0\); it does not define a zero-mass metronoid.

Third, fix \(\mathbf J\in D\). Choose finitely many components indexed by \(a\). Each component has a nonempty set \(E_a\subseteq D\) of distinct source indices, positive coefficients \(\lambda_{a,\mathbf I}\) summing to one with barycenter \(\mathbf J\), and mass \(x_a\ge0\). Allow also central mass \(x_\circ\ge0\). Define its cost by

\[
L_a=\log\frac{w_{\mathbf J}}
{\left(\sum_{\mathbf I\in E_a}
\lambda_{a,\mathbf I}w_{\mathbf I}^{1/d}\right)^d},
\qquad
\mathbf1_{\{\mathbf I=\mathbf J\}}x_\circ
+\sum_{a:\mathbf I\in E_a}x_a\le w_{\mathbf I}
\quad(\mathbf I\in D).
\tag{5}
\]

Each occurrence of a source in a component is charged the full mass \(x_a\), independently of its positive coefficient. Capacities in (5) are shared across all components, including components with the same support and different coefficients. Put \(M=x_\circ+\sum_a x_a\), and use \(S_{\mathrm{cost}}=\sum_a x_aL_a\) for the mass-weighted cost, reserving \(S\) for the locked mixed-integer set. If \(M>0\), there is a point \(\mathbf y^\star\in C_{\mathbf J}\), selected before any ambient halfspace, such that

\[
h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star))
\ge \frac{\ell M^2}{8(M\log2+S_{\mathrm{cost}})}.
\tag{6}
\]

If every positive-mass component has cost at most \(L\ge0\), there is a possibly different point \(\mathbf y^\star\in C_{\mathbf J}\) with \(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf y^\star))\ge M/[6(1+L)]\). If \(S_{\mathrm{cost}}=0\), the specific point \((\mathbf J,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J})\) satisfies \(h_S((\mathbf J,\mathbf c_{\mathbf J}))\ge\gamma_d M\). Each assertion concerns every closed ambient halfspace containing its one selected point, including vertical halfspaces. Zero-mass components may be omitted. When \(M=0\), only the trivial zero lower bound is claimed, without evaluating (6).

The entropy step used for (6) has the following precise measurable-density scope. If \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\) is a convex body, \(Q=\mathcal L^d|_K/\mathcal L^d(K)\), and \(P\) is a probability measure supported in \(K\) with a bounded measurable Lebesgue density, then \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is finite and there is \(\mathbf y^\star\in\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{supp}P)\) attaining the maximum of \(\operatorname{TD}_P\), with

\[
\operatorname{TD}_P(\mathbf y^\star)
\ge\frac{\ell}{8(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)+\log2)}.
\tag{7}
\]

Here \(\operatorname{TD}_P(\mathbf y)\) is the infimum of \(P(G)\) over proper closed halfspaces \(G\subset\mathbb R^d\) containing \(\mathbf y\). Formula (7) extends the uniform-reference specialization of accepted fact `5bd39b316ef3c194`, whose stated hypothesis requires a continuous density for \(P\). The extension is proved below without assuming such continuity.

Finally, each component in (5) can be replaced, at the same mass, by one supported on an affinely independent subset of \(E_a\) of size at most \(n+1\). Its cost and every source usage weakly decrease. For \(\mathbf J\in D\), let \(\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\) be the finite family of nonempty affinely independent subsets \(E\subseteq D\) for which \(\mathbf J\in\operatorname{relint}\operatorname{conv}E\). Its members have unique positive barycentric coefficients; let \(L_E\) be their cost in (2). The family includes \(\{\mathbf J\}\) with coefficient one and cost zero. For \(L\ge0\), define

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_d(\mathbf J,L)=\max\quad &
\sum_{\substack{E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}\\L_E\le L}}x_E\\
\text{subject to}\quad &
\sum_{\substack{E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J}:\ \mathbf I\in E\\L_E\le L}}x_E
\le w_{\mathbf I}\quad(\mathbf I\in D),\\
&x_E\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

This attained value is exactly the maximum mass of all finite schemes (5) at \(\mathbf J\) whose positive-mass components have root-volume cost at most \(L\), with central mass included. Its attained dual is

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_d(\mathbf J,L)=\min\quad &
\sum_{\mathbf I\in D}w_{\mathbf I}u_{\mathbf I}\\
\text{subject to}\quad &
\sum_{\mathbf I\in E}u_{\mathbf I}\ge1
\quad(E\in\mathcal E_{\mathbf J},\ L_E\le L),\\
&u_{\mathbf I}\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

Set \(\mathcal B_d(w)=\max_{\mathbf J\in D,\ L\ge0}P_d(\mathbf J,L)/(1+L)\). The maximum is attained, and it suffices to test the finitely many costs \(L_E\) at each target. There is one \(\mathbf p^\star\in S\) satisfying

\[
h_S(\mathbf p^\star)\ge\frac{\mathcal B_d(w)}6.
\tag{10}
\]

Consequently \(h_{\max}(C)\ge\mathcal B_d(w)/6\), with \(h_{\max}(C)=\max_{\mathbf p\in S}h_S(\mathbf p)\) as in accepted fact `03f071403cdfc69f`. If \(W=0\), set \(\mathcal B_d(w)=0\); every point in the assumed nonempty \(S\) satisfies (10), and none of the positive-volume normalizations or packing programs is required.
